note: How long each target gets on the nightly leg, and the matrix that leg builds itself from.
.github/workflows/nightly.yml reads this file with jq and fans out one job per entry, so the
target list lives in exactly one place that CI can see. FuzzGateTests.TheNightlyMatrixIsTheRegistry
asserts on every build that these names are FuzzTargets.Names in order, which is what stops a
twenty-first target from being added to the harness and quietly never fuzzed overnight.
seconds is per target and per job — the jobs run in parallel, so the nightly's wall clock is the
largest number here rather than their sum. It is a multiple of 60 because the workflow derives
timeout-minutes from it, which is the arithmetic that used to be done by hand and went stale twice.
The figures each why cites are measured, in a Release run of the case-bounded gate on an arm64
laptop: see Core/Vixen.Fuzz/README.md, The nightly's budgets. Read them as ratios — a loaded machine
reads three to four times lower across the board, and a long run is slower again as the corpus fills
with larger inputs. They are the order of magnitude a budget was chosen from, not a promise about

targets.name: packet
targets.why: 1.0 M cases/s and the bottom of every receive path. Ten minutes is ~600 M inputs, and its signature table saturates, so past that the clock buys unguided repetition rather than depth.

targets.name: bits
targets.why: 1.3 M cases/s, and saturates like packet. What replication, RPC and sync lists actually read, so it keeps the full baseline anyway.

targets.name: handshake
targets.why: 981 k cases/s over eleven distinct behaviours — a shallow decoder reached before authentication. Ten minutes is far past everything it can do.

targets.name: client
targets.why: 2.0 M cases/s, twenty behaviours. Two of the findings in this harness were a client keeping a record it should not, which is a retention oracle rather than a case count.

targets.name: snapshot
targets.why: 1.9 M cases/s. A packet that creates and destroys entities, so the interesting oracle is what the world weighs afterwards.

targets.name: inspect
targets.why: 1.1 M cases/s over 2 365 behaviours — the widest behaviour space of the byte targets, and still six hundred million inputs in ten minutes.

targets.name: delta
targets.why: 2.5 M cases/s, the fastest target here. Writes into a buffer from widths a packet chose, which is a property a billion cases will not exhaust and one bad width will show.

targets.name: rpc
targets.why: 2.4 M cases/s. Keeps 538 inputs out of 1.5 M, which is guidance working — the corpus is a selection rather than a list.

targets.name: synclist
targets.why: 540 k cases/s. The only index that arrives from the network; ten minutes is ~300 M of them.

targets.name: input
targets.why: 370 k cases/s, and its corpus is already at the 4 096 cap in the gate's own budget. Work a client can make a server do every tick.

targets.name: udp
targets.why: 251 k cases/s — a poll walks a connection table, so a case is expensive by this list's standards. The code an attacker reaches first, on a public port.

targets.name: upgrade
targets.why: 344 k cases/s over seven behaviours. Both findings here were amplification and a missing timeout rather than depth, and neither needed a long run.

targets.name: bundle
targets.why: 196 k cases/s with a CRC over the whole payload per case. Ten minutes is ~120 M opens of a file a content update downloaded.

targets.name: chunk
targets.why: 163 k cases/s, each an LZ4 or Zstd decode. A declared length that is what gets allocated, which the amplification oracle judges rather than the clock.

targets.name: heightmap
targets.why: 73 k cases/s — inflate plus an unfilter pass per case, and only 367 behaviours. A PNG somebody dropped on an importer.

targets.name: meta
targets.why: 20 k cases/s, the slowest target that is not a grammar: decode, line scan, YAML parse and a reflected bind is four passes where a packet target has one. Ten minutes is 12 M cases; thirty is 36 M, and it has an open finding.

targets.name: stylevalue
targets.why: Fills the 65 536-entry signature table and the 4 096-entry corpus inside the 3.4 s the gate spends on it. The mutator exhausts a grammar this small, so the budget is set by that rather than by 118 k cases/s.

targets.name: layerrule
targets.why: Saturates the same way in 1.3 s at 225 k cases/s. A hand-written brace matcher over text ExCSS gave up on — small, and searched out in minutes.

targets.name: vxml
targets.why: 15 k cases/s, because a case is four parses. The trailing-escape finding took 1.6 M cases, so ten minutes is five of those and an hour is fifty-five million.

targets.name: raven
targets.why: 465 cases/s — a case is a whole compiler, and the reason this leg is a matrix at all. Ten minutes is ~280 k cases and the parser hang lived at a quarter of a million, so the old shared budget was one defect deep. Two hours is ~3 M.
